akhfash:3-3.t: He said ﴿إِنَّ شَانِئَكَ هُوَ ٱلأَبْتَرُ﴾: you say "شَنِئْتَه", so "أَنا أشنَؤُهُ" "شَنَآنا" ("to hate").

celaleyn:1-1.t: ﴿إِنَّا أَعْطَيْنَاكَ﴾, O Muhammad, ﴿الْكَوْثَرَ﴾: it is a river in the Garden; it is his Pool, to which his community will come. Or al-Kawthar is the abundant good: prophethood, the Qur'an, intercession and the like.

celaleyn:2-2.t: ﴿فَصَلِّ لِرَبِّكَ﴾ the prayer of the Feast of Sacrifice ﴿وَانْحَرْ﴾ your sacrificial animal.

celaleyn:3-3.t: ﴿إِنَّ شَانِئَكَ﴾, that is, the one who hates you, ﴿هُوَ الْأَبْتَرُ﴾: the one cut off from all good, or cut off from posterity. It was revealed concerning al-ʿĀṣ ibn Wāʾil, who called the Prophet ﷺ "abtar" (cut off) at the death of his son al-Qāsim.

daas-irab:1-1.t: ﴿إِنَّا﴾ inna and its noun. ﴿أَعْطَيْناكَ﴾ a past verb, its fāʿil (agent) and its first object. ﴿الْكَوْثَرَ﴾ second mafʿūl bihi (direct object); the verbal clause is the khabar (predicate) of inna, and the nominal clause is initial (ibtidāʾiyya), with no grammatical position.

daas-irab:2-2.t: ﴿فَصَلِّ﴾ the fāʾ is a conjunction, and an imperative verb, indeclinable (mabnī) on the omission of the weak letter, and the fāʿil (agent) is latent (mustatir). ﴿لِرَبِّكَ﴾ attached to (mutaʿalliq) the verb; the clause is conjoined (maʿṭūfa) to what precedes it. ﴿وَانْحَرْ﴾ conjoined to what precedes it.

daas-irab:3-3.t: ﴿إِنَّ شانِئَكَ﴾ inna and its noun. ﴿هُوَ﴾ a pronoun of separation (ḍamīr faṣl). ﴿الْأَبْتَرُ﴾ the khabar (predicate) of inna; the nominal clause is resumptive (mustaʾnafa), with no grammatical position.

dervis-irab:1-3.t:
* Vocabulary:
(الْكَوْثَرَ) In al-Qāmūs: "Al-kawthar: the abundant of everything; the abundant, dense dust; Islam; prophethood; a village in al-Ṭāʾif where al-Ḥajjāj had a landmark; the good, generous man, like al-kathīr, as in ṣayqal; the chief; the river; and a river in Paradise from which all its rivers gush forth." The wording of al-Zamakhsharī: "Al-kawthar is of the pattern fawʿal, from kathra (abundance). It was said to a Bedouin woman whose son had returned from a journey, 'With what did your son return?' She said, 'He returned with a kawthar.' And [the poet] said:
وأنت كثير يا ابن مروان طيب ... وكان أبوك ابن العقائل كوثرا
(You are abundant, O son of Marwān, and good; and your father, the son of noble women, was a kawthar.)
The verse is by al-Kumayt; al-ʿaqāʾil are the best of women; and al-kawthar is the utmost in goodness."
The wording of Ibn Khālawayh: "Al-kawthar is a river in Paradise whose two banks are of gold, whose pebbles are coral and pearls, whose mud is musk, and whose water is whiter than snow and sweeter than honey; whoever drinks one draught of it will never thirst again. It is also said that al-kawthar is abundant good, of which the Qur'an is a part. It is of the pattern fawʿal from kathra, the wāw being redundant, like kawsaj and nawfal. Apart from this, al-kawthar is the generous man. The poet said: 'And you are abundant, O son of Marwān' (the verse)." Al-Qurṭubī cited sixteen views on al-kawthar and said that the soundest is the first, namely that it is a river in Paradise, because it is established from the Prophet ﷺ by explicit text.
(شانِئَكَ) means: the one who hates you. In al-Miṣbāḥ: "shaniʾahu, like samiʿa and manaʿa, shanʾan like falsin, and shanaʾānan with fatḥa or sukūn on the nūn: he hated him. The agent is shāniʾ for the masculine and shāniʾa for the feminine; and shaniʾtu bi-l-amr means I acknowledged it." Ibn Khālawayh said:
"Al-shāniʾ: the one who hates. Al-Aʿshā said:
ومن شانىء كاسف وجهه ... إذا ما انتسبت له أنكرن
(And [many] a hater with a gloomy face, who, when you trace your lineage to him, disowns [you].) [Translator's note: the second hemistich is rendered as it stands in the source, whose wording appears corrupt.]"
(الْأَبْتَرُ) is the one who has no posterity (ʿaqib). In origin it is a thing cut off, from batarahu, i.e., he cut it off; a ḥimār abtar is a donkey with no tail; and rajul abātir, with ḍamma on the hamza, is one who severs the ties of kinship. The wording of Ibn Khālawayh: "Its meaning is: your hater, O Muḥammad, is the abtar, that is, he has no son. Al-abtar is the insignificant; al-abtar is the abased; among snakes, al-abtar is the one with its tail cut off; and al-abtar is the tail of the elephant. The Quraysh and those who hated the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to say: 'Muḥammad is a ṣunbūr', that is, solitary, with no son, so that when he dies his memory will be cut off. So Allah, the Exalted, gave them the lie and informed them that the mention of Muḥammad is joined with the mention of Himself until the Day of Resurrection: when the muezzin says 'I testify that there is no god but Allah', he says 'I testify that Muḥammad is the Messenger of Allah'. Al-ṣunbūr is the palm tree that remains alone, with its lower part crushed. He said: A man met another man and asked him about a palm tree, and he said, 'Its lower part has withered (ṣunbura) and its top is nested in.' Al-ṣunbūr is also the iron or lead at the mouth of a water skin; and al-ṣunbūr is the small boy. Aws ibn Ḥajar said:
مخلّفون ويقضي الناس أمرهم ... غشّ الأمانة صنبور فصنبور
(Left behind, while people settle their affairs — [men] of false trust, one ṣunbūr after another.) [Translator's note: the verse is obscure and the rendering is tentative.]"
In al-Mukhtār: "Batarahu: he cut it off before completion; its pattern is naṣara; al-intibār is cutting off; al-abtar is the one with the tail cut off, of the pattern ṭariba; al-abtar is also the one who has no posterity; and every matter whose trace of good has been cut off is abtar."

* I'rab:
(إِنَّا أَعْطَيْناكَ الْكَوْثَرَ فَصَلِّ لِرَبِّكَ وَانْحَرْ) (إن) and its noun, and the clause (أعطيناك) is its khabar. In the reading of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ it was (إنّا أنطيناك) with a nūn; al-Tabrīzī said that this is a dialect of the pure Arabs, and in the ḥadīth it is said: "wa-anṭū l-thabaja", with fatḥa on the letters, meaning the middling kind between the best and the worst. (الكوثر) is a second direct object. The fāʾ is a conjunction of immediate succession. (صل) is an imperative verb, indeclinable by omission of the weak letter, and its fāʿil is a latent pronoun, its implied form being "you". (لربك) are two elements attached to (صل). The overt noun is put in place of the pronoun; the requirement would have been to say "so pray to Us", but the text shifts from the pronoun to the overt noun by way of iltifāt (grammatical shift), out of concern for the mention of "your Lord" and in magnification of Him. (وانحر) is conjoined to (صل), meaning: pray the prayer of the Day of Sacrifice. This requires the sūra to be Medinan rather than Meccan. It is also said that the command is general, covering every prayer and every sacrifice. (إِنَّ شانِئَكَ هُوَ الْأَبْتَرُ) The clause is resumptive and emphatic. (إن) and its noun; (هو) is a second mubtadaʾ or a pronoun of separation (ḍamīr faṣl); (الأبتر) is the khabar of (هو) and the clause is the khabar of (إن), or else (الأبتر) is the khabar of (إن). I do not know how Abū l-Baqāʾ permitted parsing (هو) as an emphasis (tawkīd), since an overt noun is not emphasised by a pronoun. The wording of Ibn Hishām: "Abū l-Baqāʾ erred in permitting emphasis in (إن شانئك هو الأبتر); though he may have meant that it emphasises the latent pronoun in (شانئك), not (شانئك) itself, because (شانئ) is an active participle meaning 'one who hates'."

* Rhetoric:
1- In His saying, the Exalted: «إنّا أعطيناك الكوثر فصل لربك وانحر» there is the figure of al-madhhab al-kalāmī (the argumentative style), to which reference has already been made, as it was also mentioned that one kind of it is logical, in which sound conclusions are drawn from true premises. For these two verses contain a conclusion drawn from two true premises. The explanation is that we say: the gift of al-Kawthar equals all gifts. We say this because gratitude is according to the measure of blessings, and the Messenger ﷺ was commanded to meet this blessing, in gratitude for it, with all bodily and financial acts of worship. The prayer comprises all acts of worship, so it equals all gifts. We say that what was commanded is all bodily worship because the prayer brings together standing, sitting, bowing, prostration, recitation of the Qur'an, remembrances, silence from other speech, the prohibition of food and drink, remaining in complete purity, humility, submission, supplication and entreaty; what is forbidden to the fasting person is forbidden in it — eating, drinking, intercourse, obscene talk, and all movements and stillnesses outside it. So it combines the virtues of prayer and of fasting, and works of the outward and works of the inward. Then, together with the prayer, he (peace and blessings upon him) was commanded to sacrifice (naḥr), which must mean either the Pilgrimage, which combines the two kinds of worship, or sacrifice in general, which includes the sacrifice of the offering in the Pilgrimage, the slaughter for guests, visiting neighbours, and feeding in times of hardship. It is thus clear that He, glory be to Him, commanded His Messenger ﷺ with all acts of worship in gratitude for the gift of al-Kawthar, which indicates that the gift of al-Kawthar equals all gifts. This gift had this distinction because by it he ﷺ was given excellence and glory over all the Prophets, peace be upon them, for the nations will ask their prophets to intercede for them so that they may be given to drink from the greatest thirst, and they will excuse themselves, as is reported of them in the famous, sound ḥadīth of intercession; then all the nations will find none to intercede for them or give them to drink except Muḥammad ﷺ. Observe what these two verses, brief as they are, contain of allusion: with their few words they indicate meanings which, were they expressed in the words set for them by way of elaboration, would fill pages and volumes.
2- In His saying «فصل لربك» there is an iltifāt (shift) from the first person to the third; the original would be "so pray to Us", but it departs from that because in the word "Lord" there is an urging to perform what is commanded, for the One who nurtures you deserves to be worshipped.

farraa:1-1.t:
His words, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿إِنَّآ أَعْطَيْنَاكَ ٱلْكَوْثَرَ﴾.
Ibn ʿAbbās said: It is abundant good, and the Qurʾān is part of it.
[Abū al-ʿAbbās narrated to us; he said: Muḥammad narrated to us; he said:] al-Farrāʾ narrated to us; he said: Mindal ibn ʿAlī al-ʿAnazī narrated to me, with a chain of transmission going back to ʿĀʾisha; he said: "الكوثر" is a river in Paradise; whoever would like to hear its sound, let him put his two fingers in his ears.

farraa:2-2.t:
His words, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿فَصَلِّ لِرَبِّكَ وَٱنْحَرْ﴾.
It is said: pray to your Lord on the day of the ʿĪd, then sacrifice.
[Abū al-ʿAbbās narrated to us; he said: Muḥammad narrated to us; he said:] al-Farrāʾ narrated to us; he said: Qays narrated to me from Yazīd ibn Yazīd ibn Jābir, from a man, from ʿAlī, who said concerning it: «النحر» is your holding your left hand with your right in prayer. And he said: ﴿فَصَلِّ لِرَبِّكَ وَٱنْحَرْ﴾: face the qibla with your upper chest (نحر). And I heard one of the Arabs say: منازلنا تتناحر (our dwellings face one another): this one with its front (نحر) to that one, i.e. opposite it. One of Banū Asad recited to me:
أبا حَكَم ها أنت عَمُّ مُجالِدٍ * وسيِّدُ أهلِ الأَبْطَحِ المتناحرِ
(O Abū Ḥakam, here you are, the uncle of Mujālid and the master of the people of al-Abṭaḥ, whose [dwellings] face one another.)
This is of that kind: parts of it face (ينحر) one another.

farraa:3-3.t:
His words, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿إِنَّ شَانِئَكَ هُوَ ٱلأَبْتَرُ﴾.
They used to call a man who had no male child «أبتر» (cut off) [150/b], i.e.: he dies and leaves no remembrance. Some of Quraysh said it of the Prophet ﷺ, so Allah, Blessed and Exalted is He, said: ﴿إِنَّ شَانِئَكَ﴾ — the one who hates you and is your enemy — is the «أبتر», who has no remembrance for any good deed; as for you, I have made your mention together with My mention. That is His word: ﴿وَرَفَعْنَا لَكَ ذِكْرَكَ﴾.

harrat-mujtaba:2-2.t: The clause «فصلِّ» is conjoined to the clause {أَعْطَيْنَاكَ}.

harrat-mujtaba:3-3.t: (إن شانئك هو الأبتر) [Translator's note: phrase discussed] The clause is resumptive; «هو» is a pronoun of separation (ḍamīr faṣl).

mekki-muskil:1-1.t: His saying, Exalted is He (إنا أعطيناك الكوثر): the origin of (إنا) is «إننا». One of the nūns was elided because of the gathering of like letters, and the elided one is the second, as indicated by the permissibility of eliding it in (إنّ): you say «إنْ زيد لقائم», eliding the second and leaving the first quiescent as it was. Had the elided one been the first, the second would have remained vowelled, because it was so before the elision. Eliding the third is not permissible, because it belongs to the noun [i.e. the pronoun].

muyesser-irab:1-1.t:
﴿إنا﴾: «إن» is an abrogating particle indeclinable (mabnī) on the fatḥa, with no grammatical position, and «نا» is a pronoun indeclinable on the sukūn in the position of accusative as the noun (ism) of «إن».
﴿أعطيناك﴾: a past verb indeclinable on the sukūn; «نا» is a pronoun indeclinable on the sukūn in the position of nominative as fāʿil (agent), and the kāf is a pronoun indeclinable on the fatḥa in the position of accusative as first mafʿūl bihi (direct object); the clause ﴿أعطيناك﴾ is in the position of nominative as the khabar (predicate) of «إن».
﴿الكوثر﴾: second mafʿūl bihi of ﴿أعطيناك﴾, accusative (manṣūb) by the fatḥa; the clause ﴿إنا أعطيناك الكوثر﴾ is initial (ibtidāʾiyya), with no grammatical position.

muyesser-irab:2-2.t:
﴿فصل﴾: the fāʾ is a conjunction for immediate succession (taʿqīb), and «صل» is an imperative verb indeclinable (mabnī) on the dropping of the weak letter, and its agent is latent (mustatir), its implied form being "you" (أنت).
﴿لربك﴾: the lām is a preposition, and «رب» is a noun genitive (majrūr) by the lām, the sign of its genitive being the kasra; «رب» is muḍāf, and the kāf is a pronoun indeclinable on the fatḥa in the position of genitive as muḍāf ilayhi; the preposition and its genitive noun are attached to (mutaʿalliq) ﴿صل﴾.
﴿وانحر﴾: the wāw is a conjunction, and «انحر» is an imperative verb indeclinable on the sukūn, and its agent is latent, its implied form being "you" (أنت). The clause ﴿صل...﴾ has no grammatical position, being conjoined to the one before it according to those who allow conjoining a performative (inshāʾ) clause to an informative (khabar) one, or conjoined to a resumptive clause with no grammatical position, i.e. "take heed, and pray" (انتبه فصل); and the clause ﴿انحر﴾ is conjoined to the clause ﴿صل﴾, with no grammatical position.

muyesser-irab:3-3.t:
﴿إن﴾: an abrogating particle indeclinable (mabnī) on the fatḥa, with no grammatical position.
﴿شانئك﴾: «شانئ» is the noun (ism) of «إن», accusative (manṣūb) by the fatḥa, and it is muḍāf, and the kāf is a pronoun indeclinable on the fatḥa in the position of genitive as muḍāf ilayhi.
﴿هو﴾: a pronoun indeclinable on the fatḥa, in the position of nominative as mubtadaʾ (subject).
﴿الأبتر﴾: khabar (predicate) of «هو», nominative (marfūʿ) by the ḍamma; the clause ﴿هو الأبتر﴾ is in the position of nominative as the khabar of «إن». Or: «هو» is a pronoun of separation (ḍamīr faṣl), and «الأبتر» is the khabar of «إن», nominative by the ḍamma. The clause ﴿إن شانئك هو الأبتر﴾ is resumptive, with no grammatical position.

nahhas-irab:1-1.t: The first nūn and alif (in إنّا) are in the position of the accusative as the ism of إنّ, and the latter (in أعطينا) are in the position of the nominative. الْكَوْثَرَ is a second object. In the language it is fawʿal from kathra (abundance). The scholars have differed on its meaning. From the Prophet ﷺ: that it is the Pool (al-ḥawḍ). And when Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said: al-Kawthar is abundant good, it was said to him: "But it has been said that it is the Pool", and he said: "The Pool is part of the abundant good". Al-Ḥasan and Qatāda said: al-Kawthar is the Qur'an. And it was read before Muḥammad ibn Jaʿfar ibn Ḥafṣ, from Yūsuf ibn Mūsā: ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Mūsā narrated to us: Shuʿba narrated to us, from ʿUmāra ibn Abī Ḥafṣa, from ʿIkrima, who said: «إِنَّا أَعْطَيْناكَ الْكَوْثَرَ» (1): he said: prophethood and the Qur'an.

nahhas-irab:2-2.t:
The scholars have differed on its meaning. Among the most important of that is what Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Jaʿfar narrated to us, saying: Abū Bakr ibn (Abī) Shayba narrated to us: Wakīʿ narrated to us, from Yazīd ibn Abī Ziyāda ibn Abī al-Jaʿd [Translator's note: so in the text], from ʿĀṣim al-Jaḥdarī, from ʿUqba ibn Ẓuhayr, from ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, may Allah be pleased with him, concerning the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: فَصَلِّ لِرَبِّكَ وَانْحَرْ (2): he said: (it is) placing the right (hand) on the left in prayer.
Abū Jaʿfar said: There is disagreement in what is narrated from him about that. It is narrated from him that he said: he places the right (hand) on the left forearm upon his chest; and from him and from Abū Hurayra: he puts them below the navel, and this is the position of the Kufans. The first view is argued for on the basis that it is closer to the verse, because the meaning of وانحر is "put your hand toward your upper chest (naḥr)". Sufyān narrated, (and) Shuʿba [Translator's note: the text reads «لشعبة»], from ʿĀṣim ibn Kulayb, from his son [Translator's note: so in the text; the known chain is "from his father"], from Wāʾil ibn Ḥujr; he said: I saw the Prophet ﷺ — "put your hand toward your upper chest" [Translator's note: the text appears to be disrupted here]. And Sufyān and Shuʿba narrated, from ʿĀṣim ibn Anas [Translator's note: so in the text], from Abū Ḥāzim, from Sahl ibn Saʿd, who said: people used to be commanded that a man should place his right hand on the left in prayer. Abū Jaʿfar said: On this view, "so pray to your Lord" means all the prayers, and "and naḥr" means put your hand toward your naḥr [Translator's note: the text reads «نحوك»]. This is one view.
From Abū Jaʿfar Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī: وَانْحَرْ means raise your hand toward your upper chest when you say the takbīr for entering prayer. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: وَانْحَرْ means "and ask". A fourth view: «وانحر» means face the qibla with your upper chest, as is reported from the Arabs: "the two are facing each other (yatanāḥarān)", i.e., fighting each other. Abū Jaʿfar said:
This is not the view of anyone among the early scholars. A fifth view, from Anas ibn Mālik: The Prophet used to sacrifice and then pray, until فصلّ لربك وانحر was revealed, after which he would pray and then sacrifice. A sixth view, held by most of the Successors: al-Ḥasan and ʿAṭāʾ said: i.e., pray the ʿĪd (prayer) and slaughter the sacrificial camels. Abū Jaʿfar said: This is the view of Mujāhid and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, and it is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him. Some of the people of reasoning incline to it, because it is the apparent meaning, i.e., slaughter the camels by naḥr (stabbing at the base of the neck), and do not slaughter them by dhabḥ. Some of the jurists reject it, because the ʿĪd prayer is not obligatory according to any of the Muslims, and the sacrifice (uḍḥiya) is not obligatory according to most scholars, as it is narrated that Abū Bakr and ʿUmar used not to sacrifice, for fear that people would imagine it to be obligatory; and likewise Ibn ʿAbbās said: I have not sacrificed except with meat I bought.
There is a seventh view on the verse, and it is the clearest of them: it is the position of Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb, who said: make your prayer sincerely for Allah and sacrifice for Him alone. This is a good view, because Allah, Mighty and Majestic, made known to him what He had honoured him with and given him, and then commanded him to thank Him for that, so that he would not do as the idolaters do, and that his prayer would be sincerely for Allah alone and his sacrifice intended for what is with Allah, Mighty and Majestic — not as the disbelievers do.

nahhas-irab:3-3.t: إِنَّ شانِئَكَ: Ibn ʿAbbās said: (it is) your enemy Abū Jahl; and it has been said: al-ʿĀṣī ibn Wāʾil. هُوَ الْأَبْتَرُ, i.e., the one cut off from mention with good; no one stands [Translator's note: the text reads «يا قوم», evidently for «يقوم»] by his religion, and no one mentions him with good. This was among the signs of his prophethood ﷺ, that he informed of what had not happened, and it was as he informed. It has been said: when Allah revealed إِنَّ شانِئَكَ هُوَ الْأَبْتَرُ (3), no child was born to him (al-ʿĀṣī) after that; but the first is more correct. Its origin is from batarahu, i.e., he cut it off.

safi-cedvel:1-3.t:
* I'rab:
(the fāʾ) is a conjunction for causal connection. (لربّك) is attached to (صلّ). (هو) is a separating pronoun (ḍamīr faṣl) [Note: or a detached pronoun in the position of nominative, a mubtadaʾ whose khabar is الأبتر, the nominal clause being the khabar of إنّ.].
Clause: «إنّا أعطيناك ... » has no grammatical position; it is inceptive.
And the clause: «أعطيناك ... » is in the position of nominative, the khabar of إنّ.
And the clause: «صلّ ... » has no grammatical position; it is conjoined to an implied resumption, i.e. "take note of this, so pray" [Note: it is possible for the clause to be the response to an implied condition.].
And the clause: «انحر ... » has no grammatical position; it is conjoined to the clause صلّ.
And the clause: «إنّ شانئك هو الأبتر» has no grammatical position; it is resumptive.

* Morphology:
(الكوثر): a proper name of a river in Paradise; its wazn is فوعل, from الكثرة (abundance). The Arabs call everything of great number or of great worth and importance a kawthar; or it is an adjective of an omitted described noun, i.e. "the abundant good" (al-khayr al-kawthar).. In exegesis there are sixteen opinions on the meaning of al-Kawthar.. such as the Pond, prophethood, the Qur'an ... etc.
(شانئك): an active participle from شنأ meaning "to hate"; its wazn is فاعل.
(الأبتر): a ṣifa mushabbaha (assimilated adjective) from بتر meaning "to cut" (class of نصر, transitive), and from the class of فرح meaning "to be cut off" (intransitive); its wazn is أفعل, i.e. one whose line of descent is cut off.

* Rhetoric:
1- The art of al-madhhab al-kalāmī (the argumentative method): in His saying, the Exalted: «إِنَّا أَعْطَيْناكَ الْكَوْثَرَ».
Al-madhhab al-kalāmī has several kinds; one is a logical kind in which sound conclusions are drawn from true premises. These two verses contain a conclusion from two true premises, and the explanation is that we say: the bestowal of al-Kawthar equals all bestowals, and we say so because gratitude is in proportion to the favours; and the Messenger ﷺ was commanded to meet this favour with all acts of worship, bodily and financial, in gratitude for it. Prayer comprises many acts of worship; then he, upon him be blessings and peace, was commanded, along with prayer, to sacrifice (naḥr), and it must be that what is meant by it is the Hajj, which comprises some acts of worship. What these two verses, despite their brevity, contain of allusion, indicating by few words meanings which, if expressed by the words assigned to them in the way of elaboration, would fill pages and volumes.
2- Iltifāt (shift of person): in His saying, the Exalted: «فَصَلِّ لِرَبِّكَ».
In this shift from the pronoun of majesty to the specific "Lord", annexed to his pronoun, upon him be blessings and peace, there is reinforcement of the encouragement of him ﷺ to perform what he was commanded in the most perfect manner.
3- Metaphor (istiʿāra): in His saying, the Exalted: «إِنَّ شانِئَكَ هُوَ الْأَبْتَرُ».
One who has no descendants is called abtar by way of metaphor, where the child and the remaining trace are likened to the tail, since it is behind him, as though it comes after him, and its absence is his absence.

* Benefits:
The Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited this sūra, then said to his Companions: Do you know what al-Kawthar is? We said: Allah and His Messenger know best. He said: It is a river that my Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, promised me, with much good in it; it is a pond to which my community will come on the Day of Resurrection; its vessels are as many as the stars of the sky. A servant of them will be driven away, and I will say: My Lord, he is of my community. He will say: You do not know what he innovated after you. This is the wording of Muslim. And al-Bukhārī said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: When I was taken up to the heaven, I came to a river whose two banks had domes of hollow pearl. I said: What is this, O Jibrīl? He said: This is al-Kawthar which your Lord has given you. And behold, its clay was fragrant musk. On the authority of Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was asked, What is al-Kawthar? He said: That is a river which Allah gave me – meaning in Paradise – whiter than milk and sweeter than honey. In it are birds whose necks are like the necks of camels. ʿUmar said: These are delightful. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: Those who eat them are more delightful than they. Reported by al-Tirmidhī, who said: a good, sound ḥadīth. [Translator's note: the source reads "قال عمران" (ʿImrān); translated as written.]

semin-durr:1-1.t:
His saying: {أَعْطَيْنَاكَ}: al-Ḥasan, Ibn Muḥayṣin, Ṭalḥa and al-Zaʿfarānī read «اَنْطَيْناك». Al-Rāzī and al-Tabrīzī said: "He substituted nūn for the ʿayn." If they meant a technical substitution (al-badal al-ṣināʿī), that is not conceded, because each of the two roots stands on its own, as shown by the completeness of their conjugations; but if by substitution they meant that this one took the place of that one in the language, it is close, and there is no doubt that it is an established dialect. Al-Tabrīzī said: "It is the dialect of the pure Arabs, of the first Quraysh." In the hadith from him ﷺ: "The upper hand is the giving (al-munṭiya), and the lower hand is the receiving (al-munṭāh)." The poet said, and he is al-Aʿshā:
4658 - جِيادُك خيرُ جيادِ الملُوك ... تُصان الجِلالَ وتُنْطِي الشَّعيرا
(Your thoroughbreds are the best of the kings' thoroughbreds; they are kept covered with horse-cloths and given barley.)
Al-kawthar is of the pattern fawʿal from "abundance" (al-kathra), an attribute of intensity for what is excessive in abundance. The poet said:
4659 - وأنت كثيرُ با بنَ مروانَ طَيِّبٌ ... وكان ابوكَ ابنَ العَقائلِ كَوْثَرا
(You, son of Marwān, are abundant and good, and your father was a son of noble women, a kawthar.)
A Bedouin woman was asked about her son: "With what did your son return?" She said: "He returned with a kawthar", that is, with much good.

semin-durr:2-2.t: His saying: {وانحر}: an imperative from "naḥr", which for camels is the equivalent of slaughter (dhabḥ) for cattle and sheep. It was also said: "Place your hands at your throat, or beneath your throat, in the prayer." Al-shāniʾ is the one who hates (al-mubghiḍ). One says "shaniʾahu, yashnaʾuhu", that is, he hated him. This was treated earlier in [Sūrat] al-Māʾida.

semin-durr:3-3.t:
His saying: {هُوَ الأبتر}: «هو» may be a mubtadaʾ, with «الأبترُ» as its khabar and the sentence as the khabar of «إنَّ»; or it may be a separating pronoun (faṣl). Abū l-Baqāʾ said: "or an emphasis (tawkīd)", but that is a mistake on his part, because a noun that is overt is not emphasised by a pronoun. Al-abtar is the one who has no posterity (ʿaqib); in origin it is the thing cut off, from "batarahu", that is, he cut it off. "A donkey abtar" is one with no tail. "A man ubātir", with ḍamma on the hamza, is one who cuts his kinship ties. He said:
4660 - لَئيمٌ نَزَتْ في أَنْفِه خُنْزُوانَةٌ ... على قَطْعِ ذي القربى أَحَدُّ أُباتِرُ
(A base man, in whose nose arrogance has leapt, over the cutting of the kinsman, a sharp ubātir.)
And "batira", with kasra, he: his tail was cut off.
The majority read «شانِئَك» with alif, an active participle (ism fāʿil) with the sense of the present, the future or the past. Ibn ʿAbbās read «شَنِئَك» without alif. It was said that it may be a form of intensity, like faʿʿāl and mifʿāl; Sībawayh affirmed it and recited:
4661 - حَذِرٌ أُموراً لا تَضِيرُ وآمِنُ ... ما ليسَ مُنْجِيَه من الأقْدارِ
(Wary of matters that do no harm, and feeling safe from what will not save him from the decrees.)
And Zayd al-Khayl said:
4662 - أتاني أنهم مَزِقون عِرْضي ... جِحاشٌ الكِرْمَلَيْنِ لها فَديدُ
(It reached me that they are tearing my honour, the foals of the two Kirmals, with a loud noise.)
If it has the sense of the present or the future, its annexation to its object is an annexation in the sense of the accusative (min naṣb); and if it has the sense of the past, it is not in the sense of the accusative. It was also said that it may be a shortened form of the active participle, as they say "barr" and "bārr", "baridh" and "bārid".
His saying: {فَصَلِّ}: the fāʾ is for succession and causation (li-l-taʿqīb wa-l-tasabbub), that is: from this great favour, and following it, there follows your command to devote yourself to the worship of the One who has favoured you and to turn to Him with sacrifice, not as Quraysh do, with their prayer and their sacrifice to their idols.
The people of knowledge said: this sūra, though it is the shortest sūra in the Qurʾān, contains eloquent meanings and wonderful modes of expression, twenty-two in number. The first: the indication of the opening of the sūra that it is a giving of much from the Much. The second: the attribution of the verb to the speaker who magnifies himself. The third: its presentation in the past form, to affirm its occurrence, like {أتى أَمْرُ الله} [al-Naḥl: 1]. The fourth: the emphasis of the sentence with «إنَّ». The fifth: building the verb upon the noun, to give the attribution twice. The sixth: the use of a form that indicates intensity of abundance. The seventh: the omission of the one described by al-kawthar, because in omitting it there is an excess of generality and vagueness that is not there in expressing it. The eighth: its definiteness by the generic al-, which indicates inclusiveness. The ninth: the fāʾ of succession, which, as stated earlier, indicates causation, for favour is a cause of thanks and worship. The tenth: the allusion to those whose prayer and sacrifice are for other than Allah the Exalted. The eleventh: that the command to pray is a pointer to the religious works of which prayer is the mainstay and the best, and the command to sacrifice a pointer to the bodily works of which sacrifice is the loftiest. The twelfth: the omission of what «انحَرْ» relates to, for the implied form is "pray to your Lord and sacrifice to Him". The thirteenth: the observance of rhymed prose (sajʿ), which is among the arts of badīʿ free from affectation. The fourteenth: His saying {رَبِّك}: in bringing this attribute rather than the rest of His beautiful attributes there is an indication that He is the one who sets right for him, who nurtures his favours, so seek every good only from Him. The fifteenth: the shift (iltifāt) from the first-person pronoun to the third person in His saying «لربِّك». The sixteenth: making the command to leave off concern for his hater a resumption, and making it the conclusion of the turning away from the hater; and He did not name him, so as to include everyone who is described, may Allah protect us, with this ugly attribute, even though a specific person is meant by it. The seventeenth: the alert, by mentioning this ugly attribute, that he is described by it only in the mere subsistence of the attribute in him, without having any effect whatever on the one he hates, because one who hates a person may sometimes have an effect on him by his hatred. The eighteenth: the emphasis of the sentence with «إنَّ», which signals emphasis of the report, and for this reason the oath is answered by it, and the implication of an oath is suitable here. The nineteenth: the use of the separating pronoun, which signals specification and emphasis, if we make «هو» a separating pronoun, and if we make it a mubtadaʾ it likewise gives emphasis, since the attribution becomes twofold. The twentieth: the definiteness of «الأبتر» with al-, which signals specificity to this attribute, as if it had been said: "the perfect in this attribute". The twenty-first: the use of the form afʿal, which indicates the utmost in this attribute. The twenty-second: His turning to His Messenger ﷺ with address from the beginning of the sūra to its end.

ukberi-tibyan:2-3.t:
Allah the Exalted said: (فَصَلِّ لِرَبِّكَ وَانْحَرْ (٢) إِنَّ شَانِئَكَ هُوَ الْأَبْتَرُ (٣)).
The words of the Exalted (فَصَلِّ): the fāʾ is for immediate sequence (taʿqīb), i.e. right after the completion of the prayer. (هُوَ) is a mubtadaʾ (subject), or a tawkīd (emphasis), or a separating pronoun (faṣl). And Allah knows best.

zajjaj:1-1.t:
Sūrat al-Kawthar
Meccan
﷽
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿إنّا أعْطَيْناكَ الكَوْثَرَ﴾ ("We have given you al-Kawthar"): it has come in the exegesis that al-Kawthar is a river in Paradise, whiter than milk and sweeter than honey, its two banks domes of hollow pearl. And it has also come in the exegesis that al-Kawthar is Islam and prophethood. The lexicographers said: al-Kawthar is on the pattern ”فَوْعَلٌ“ from ”اَلْكَثْرَةُ“ ("abundance"), and its meaning is ”اَلْخَيْرُ الكَثِيرُ“ ("abundant good"). Everything that has come in the explanation of this has been given to the Prophet, peace be upon him: he was given Islam, prophethood, the manifesting of the religion he brought over every religion, victory over his enemy, intercession, and countless things that he was given; and he has been given of Paradise according to the measure of his excellence over the people of Paradise.

zajjaj:2-2.t: And the meaning of ﴿فَصَلِّ لِرَبِّكَ وانْحَرْ﴾ ("so pray to your Lord and sacrifice"): that is, and sacrifice also for your Lord. And it was said: "By it the morning prayer on the Day of Sacrifice is meant", that is: and sacrifice after the dawn prayer. What has come most is that ”فَصَلِّ لِرَبِّكَ وانْحَرْ“ is the prayer of the Day of al-Aḍḥā, then the sacrifice after the prayer. And it was said: ﴿فَصَلِّ لِرَبِّكَ وانْحَرْ﴾ means: place your right hand on your left when you stand in prayer, and hold them to your chest (naḥr).

zajjaj:3-3.t: And His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿إنَّ شانِئَكَ هو الأبْتَرُ﴾ ("it is your hater who is cut off"): ”شانِئَكَ“ means "the one who hates you". This is al-ʿĀṣ ibn Wāʾil: the Prophet, peace be upon him, came in while he was sitting, and he said: "This is the abtar", that is: this is the one who has no posterity. So Allah the Exalted said: ﴿إنَّ شانِئَكَ﴾, O Muhammad, ﴿هُوَ الأبْتَرُ﴾. It may be "he is the one whose posterity is cut off", and it may be "he is the one cut off from every good". And ”اَلْبَتْرُ“ is cutting off from the root.
